sysd-msg-036.title: Apache Kafka: a log that keeps messages after they are read
sysd-msg-036.text: Most queues hand a message over and forget it. Kafka keeps it. Apache Kafka is an open-source distributed platform, written in Java and Scala, for storing events and processing streams of them. Unlike queue-based systems, it retains messages in a durable, append-only log until they expire. So multiple consumers can read at different offsets, which are positions in the log, and pull at their own pace. The project aims to provide a unified, high-throughput, low-latency platform for handling real-time data feeds. Kafka can handle multiple producers and consumers, with disk-based data retention and high scalability. Ordering is guaranteed within each partition, one of the parts a topic is split into, but not across the entire topic. Kafka Connect moves data in and out of external systems, and the libraries of {{ref:sysd-msg-040}} support stream-processing applications. Kafka was originally built for massive log processing. It is used for log analysis, data streaming such as recommendations, watching systems and raising alerts, and carrying database changes elsewhere, a job that {{ref:sysd-msg-041}} describes. Kafka Raft (KRaft) uses the Raft algorithm for metadata management.

sysd-msg-133.title: Batch processing: jobs that run unattended
sysd-msg-133.text: Some work is best done with nobody at the keyboard. Batch processing is the running of a software job in an automated and unattended way. A user schedules a job, and a processing system runs it, typically at a configured time of day, when an event occurs or when computer resources are available. It collects data and processes it all at once, as in daily billing. The alternative handles data in real time, as in fraud detection, and {{ref:sysd-msg-043}} takes it up. Batch applications stay critical because many business processes suit them and online systems are not optimized for high-volume repetitive tasks. They update information at day's end, generate reports and print documents by business deadlines. If a job needs only one input at a time, flow processing lowers latency per input. If it needs totals over all records, the whole batch must finish before any result is usable. A batch window is a period of less-intensive online activity in which batch jobs can run without interfering with interactive systems. It shrank as demands for online uptime grew.

sysd-msg-043.title: Stream processing, where the data never ends
sysd-msg-043.text: A batch job, as in {{ref:sysd-msg-133}}, knows where its data ends. A stream does not. Stream processing, also called event stream processing, is a programming paradigm. It treats streams, or sequences of events in time, as the central input and output objects of computation. It encompasses dataflow programming, reactive programming and distributed data processing. The data is an unbounded, continuous sequence of elements rather than a static dataset. A series of operations called kernel functions is applied to each element, and uniform streaming, where one kernel function applies to all elements, is typical. The program defines a dataflow sequence, and the execution environment applies the kernel automatically as new elements arrive. Kernels can also do aggregation windows or stateful modifications. Applying the same function to every record lets many records be processed at once. The paradigm sacrifices some flexibility for easier, faster and more efficient execution. It works well for data-centric workloads but less well for general-purpose processing with random data access, such as databases.

sysd-msg-132.title: Apache Spark: analytics without the trips to disk
sysd-msg-132.text: Spark exists because MapReduce kept going back to disk. Apache Spark is an open-source unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing. MapReduce, from {{ref:sysd-scale-040}}, forces a linear dataflow that reads from disk and writes results to disk. Spark's foundation is the resilient distributed dataset, or RDD, a read-only multiset spread over a cluster. RDDs are immutable, their operations are lazy, and lost data is rebuilt from each RDD's lineage. They suit iterative algorithms and interactive analysis, cutting latency by orders of magnitude versus Hadoop MapReduce. Spark manages the workflow as a directed acyclic graph in which nodes are RDDs and edges are the operations on them. Its streaming ingests data in micro-batches, so batch code can be reused for streaming. The cost is a latency penalty equal to the micro-batch duration, while Storm and Flink process event by event. Libraries on Spark Core include MLlib for distributed machine learning and GraphX for graph processing, though GraphX is unsuitable for graphs that must be updated.

sysd-msg-037.title: Topics, partitions, brokers and consumer groups
sysd-msg-037.text: Kafka's design comes down to a few moving parts. The message is the basic unit of data, like a record in a table, consisting of headers, a key and a value. Every message goes to a topic, which is like a folder on a computer, and topics have multiple partitions. Producers create new messages, batch them, send them to a topic and balance them across the partitions. Consumers work together as a consumer group to read messages from the broker. A Kafka cluster consists of several brokers, and each partition is replicated across multiple brokers to ensure high availability and redundancy. Partitions also give fault isolation and parallel processing: a consumer that delays committing an offset stalls only its own partition while the others remain unaffected. In 2025 Kafka added share groups as an alternative to consumer groups. They give queue-like semantics with individual acknowledgment and allow more consumers than partitions, where consumer groups assign each partition exclusively.

sysd-msg-038.title: How Kafka can still lose a message
sysd-msg-038.text: Many developers believe Kafka by design guarantees no message loss. Its architecture and configuration decide how and when it might lose messages, and there are three places to look: the producer, the broker and the consumer. On the producer side, producer.send() does not send directly to the broker. The application thread puts the message in a record accumulator. A separate sender thread then sends it, so proper acks and retries settings are needed to make sure messages arrive. On the broker side, a healthy cluster should not lose messages. But they are usually flushed to disk asynchronously for higher I/O throughput, so an instance that goes down before the flush loses them. Replicas, covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-043}}, must be properly configured to hold a valid copy of the data. On the consumer side, auto-committing might acknowledge records before they are processed, so a consumer that goes down mid-processing can leave some records never processed. A good practice combines asynchronous commits in the processing loop for throughput with synchronous commits in exception handling, so the last offset is always committed.

sysd-msg-040.title: Kafka Streams: stream processing as a Java library
sysd-msg-040.text: Kafka Streams is a library written in Java for stateful stream-processing applications that are scalable, elastic and fault-tolerant. Its main API is a domain-specific language with high-level operators such as filter, map, grouping, windowing, aggregation, joins and tables. A lower-level Processor API implements custom operators and can be mixed with it. For stateful processing it keeps local operator state in RocksDB, which can write to disk, so the state can be larger than main memory. To survive failures, every update to the local state stores is also written to a topic in the Kafka cluster. The state can then be recreated by reading those topics back into RocksDB.

sysd-msg-045.title: Complex event processing: spotting the pattern in the events
sysd-msg-045.text: Three small events, blowOutTire, zeroSpeed and driverLeftSeat, in a short time signal an accident, though no single measurement shows it. That is complex event processing: techniques for extracting information from event streams as they arrive, to identify meaningful events such as opportunities or threats. A complex or composite event is inferred from simpler constituent events, as bells, a tuxedo, a gown and rice signal a wedding. The techniques include detecting causality, membership or timing relationships between events. They also include continuous SQL queries over timestamps and windows, such as joining stock orders to trades matched within one second. Typical uses are stock trading and credit-card fraud detection.

sysd-msg-041.title: Change data capture: copying database changes elsewhere
sysd-msg-041.text: Databases drift out of sync. Constant data changes leave databases, data lakes and data warehouses disagreeing, and change data capture, or CDC, replicates and syncs data across systems to overcome this. It is a set of design patterns for determining and tracking data that changed. The source is the system with data believed to have changed, and the target is the system that needs to act on the changed data. A CDC tool monitors the database transaction logs through a source connector to capture inserts, updates and deletes. The changes are transformed, published to a message queue and propagated to targets such as data warehouses, analytics platforms and distributed caches like Redis. There a sink connector consumes the log and updates the targets in real time. A popular solution uses Debezium with Kafka Connect to stream changes from source to target, with Kafka as the broker. In the push model the source creates a snapshot of changes and delivers rows downstream. In the pull model the downstream target requests the data from the source.

sysd-msg-042.title: Three ways to detect that a row has changed
sysd-msg-042.text: Three families of methods notice that data has changed. The first uses extra columns. With a timestamp column, any row stamped more recently than the last capture is considered changed. With version numbers, changed rows are marked with a version. At capture all data with the latest version is considered changed, and the reference table then gets a new version number. A status column can mark a row as changed. It can also complement the other methods by showing that a row with a new version or later date should not yet be updated on the target. Using time, version and status together is a particularly powerful mechanism, because the three elements are not redundant. The second family uses triggers. Events on the transactional table are logged into a queue table that can later be played back to replicate the data to a target. The third reads the database transaction log. That has minimal impact on the database, needs no application changes, and can replay the original transactions in the order they were committed. It is hard, though. No standard exists for the log format, most databases do not document it, and uncommitted changes later rolled back must be eliminated.

sysd-msg-044.title: Three execution models for stream engines
sysd-msg-044.text: Stream engines differ mainly in how they run. Distributed stream processing engines are grouped by execution model into native continuous engines, micro-batch engines and distributed logging fabrics. Native continuous engines process elements individually as they arrive, optimizing for sub-second, real-time latencies; Apache Storm, Flink (see {{ref:sysd-msg-131}}) and Apache Samza belong here. Micro-batch engines collect incoming elements into small time windows to achieve high-throughput stream semantics, as Apache Spark Streaming does with live data in small discrete chunks. Distributed logging fabrics, such as Apache Kafka, serve as the persistent, append-only transport layer. Managed services such as AWS Kinesis and Google Cloud Dataflow run streams in the cloud.

sysd-msg-131.title: Apache Flink: one engine for batches and streams
sysd-msg-131.text: Flink runs batch and stream programs on the same engine. Apache Flink is an open-source, unified stream-processing and batch-processing framework. Its core is a distributed streaming dataflow engine, and its pipelined runtime executes both kinds of program, processing events one at a time on finite and infinite datasets. A dataflow starts at sources such as a message queue or file system, applies any number of transformations, and ends at sinks. The streams form a directed acyclic graph that can branch and merge. Checkpoints are automatic asynchronous snapshots of application state and source stream position. After a failure Flink resumes from the last completed checkpoint, which gives exactly-once state semantics within an application. Savepoints are manually triggered checkpoints. A user can stop a program and resume it from the same state and stream position. That allows updates without losing state and, since Flink 1.2, a change of parallelism. Flink has no storage system of its own, so it provides source and sink connectors to systems such as Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, HDFS, Apache Cassandra and Elasticsearch.

sysd-msg-039.title: Why Kafka is fast: sequential writes and zero copy
sysd-msg-039.text: Kafka turns a bursty stream of random message writes into linear ones. Its message-set abstraction groups messages, which leads to larger network packets and larger sequential disk operations. That reliance on sequential I/O is one of two design decisions that carry the most weight in Kafka's performance; the other is the zero-copy principle. Without zero copy, data is loaded from disk to the OS cache, copied to the Kafka application, copied to the socket buffer, then copied to the network card. With zero copy, the OS cache copies the data directly to the network card via the sendfile() command, saving multiple copies between the application and kernel contexts.

openers.event-streaming-and-kafka: Some messaging systems keep every message instead of discarding it after delivery. Apache Kafka does this: it stores messages in a durable log, so many consumers can read them. This chapter starts with jobs that run in an automated and unattended way, then moves to treating streams of events as the central input and output of computation. Along the way it looks at how Kafka organizes its data and how it can still lose messages, at engines that process streams, and at ways of copying database changes into other systems.

reviews.message-queues-and-brokers: A message queue lets sender and receiver work at different moments, and a broker adds translation, storage and routing between them. What a consumer can rely on depends on the delivery semantics, on features such as dead letter queues, and on the protocol, which is why choosing a queue means comparing all of them. Publish–subscribe changes the shape: every subscriber of a topic gets each message, which gains decoupling but makes delivery harder to guarantee. Event streaming platforms trade delivery tracking, fault-tolerance features and routing for scale.
reviews.event-streaming-and-kafka: Kafka keeps messages in a durable log split into partitions, so many consumers can read them, yet it can still lose a message at the producer, the broker or the consumer unless acknowledgments, replicas and offset commits are set with care. Sequential disk writes and zero copy explain much of its speed. Batch processing waits for all the data, stream processing handles it as it arrives, and engines such as Spark and Flink differ in whether they work in micro-batches or event by event. Complex event processing infers bigger events from small ones, and change data capture carries database changes into other systems by reading transaction logs, using triggers or comparing columns.
